Amyotrophic Lateral 
Sclerosis (ALS)
Adela Parola, Joshua Ervilus, Atolani Azeez, 
Aliza Brown, Vanessa Familia, Sarah Israel, 
Michelle Flores

Neurodegenerative disease of unknown cause involving  
loss of motor neurons  in the spinal cord  and brain stem .
 
Nerve cells die
Impaired nerve signals
Motor neuron degeneration  
Amytrophic Lateral Sclerosis
 “Lou Gehrig disease”
Muscle weakness
Poor communication 
brain-muscles
Muscle atrophy

Risk Factors
 Prevention
• Age (~40-60 yo) of all ethnic 
backgrounds
• Males affected > Females
• Hx of autoimmune disease
• Environmental exposures to toxins
• Excessive alcohol consumption 
• Family history (10-15% are familial) 
• Genetics (autosomal dominant trait 
carried by one parent) 
• Low BMI
• Smoking
• Viral Infections
Lifestyle changes that may help prevent 
ALS:
    Smoking cessation
    Limiting environmental toxins 
(pesticides, lead)
    SCI/TBI Prevention by wearing 
protective gear during contact sports

Health Promotion
RN's help promote wellness for ALS patients by:
 ROM exercises 
 Encourage increased daily fluid intake
 Encourage a diet high in fiber and use stool softeners to aid in motility 
 Patient education on signs and symptoms of illness/progression to notify MD
__________________________________________________________________
Consult with interdisciplinary team:  
Speech Therapist  - to speak with weakened muscles
Physical Therapist  - exercise techniques to strengthen muscles
Occupational Therapist  - use assistive devices (ex. electric toothbrush)
Mental health support  - cope with living with ALS

Early Detection & Clinical Manifestations
• Fatigue
• Progressive muscle weakness
• Cramps 
• Progressive fasciculations 
• Worsening lack of coordination
• Gradual muscle weakness - (arms, legs or hands)
• Lack of coordination  - tripping or difficulty walking
• Muscle cramps 
• Fasciculations (small, involuntary 
muscle twitching) 
• New difficulty with ADLs
• Change in speech or swallowing 
 
Early Signs To Recognize 
• Dysarthria (difficulty with speech)
• Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing)
• Respiratory changes; airway 
protection and airway clearance
• Impaired ability to laugh, cough, or 
even blow the nose
Clinical Manifestations

Electromyography (EMG) and conduction studies  help detect loss of motor units and nerve damage. 
EMG can also help rule out conditions that may present similarly to ALS (Štětkářová & Ehler, 2021).
Before EMG: 
• Nurse must verify informed consent
• Educate patient to avoid smoking & caffeine 
• Instruct patients not to apply any skin creams/oils as it can interfere with conduction 
• Ensure that provider is aware of any implants, medical devices, or blood thinners
During EMG:
• Ensure patient is positioned with head up to maintain airway
• Monitor respiratory status 
• Provide emotional support/relaxation techniques
• Help position and use supports as needed for comfort
After EMG:
• Assess needle sites for signs of bleeding or hematomas 
• Provide analgesics & muscle relaxants as prescribed 
• Provide psychosocial support 
• Ensure patient comfort through proper positioning and support
ALS is diagnosed based on signs and symptoms as there is no laboratory tests specific to this disease 
Diagnostic Tests

Medical/Medication 
Management & Nursing 
Responsibilities of ALS
• Goal: maintain/improve function, well-being, and quality of 
life
• Most patients with ALS are managed at home and in the 
community with hospitalization for acute problems.
• Disease-modifying therapy: Riluzole (may extend survival) , 
Edaravone (may slow functional decline)
• Baclofen, dantrolene sodium, or diazepam  may be useful 
for patients troubled by spasticity
• Modafinil  may be used for fatigue 
• Respiratory support : Noninvasive positive-pressure 
ventilation; mechanical ventilation (if alveolar 
hypoventilation develops)
• Nutritional support:  enteral feeding/PEG
• Multidisciplinary rehabilitation and supportive care
(Hinkle et al., 2025)
Medical Management of ALS Nursing Responsibilities for ALS
• Monitor respiratory status  and airway protection
• Assess swallowing and aspiration risk
• Monitor nutrition, hydration, and weight
• Promote mobility, independence, and functional 
ability
• Monitor medication effects and symptom control
• Address psychosocial and emotional needs 
related to progressive loss of function
• Provide emotional support and involve 
patient/family in care decisions
• Educate patient and caregivers about disease 
progression and available support resources
• Encourage advance directives and goals-of-care 
discussions
(Hinkle et al., 2025)

Recognizing these problems at home allows for early intervention 
• Dehydration
• Malnutrition
• Pneumonia
• Respiratory Failure
End-of-life issues include pain, dyspnea, and delirium
• Safety and mobility concerns; changes in mobility, frequent falls, or difficulty transferring in and OOB or chairs.
• Provide continuous care as it is unsafe for patient with ALS to REMAIN HOME ALONE for extended periods.
• Resources for caregivers as caregiver burnout is common due to overwhelming caregiving and household management duties.
• Emphasize need for specialized equipment; hospital beds, lifts, wheelchairs, or speech devices.
• Recent medical events, such as hospital stays, surgeries, or the need for skilled nursing, physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech 
therapy.. 
Patient + Family Education
 Discharge Planning 
• Allow life-support measures to made by 
the patient and family
• Patients are encouraged to complete an 
Advance Directive to preserve their 
autonomy
• Ensure that patient and caregiver have thorough 
understanding of the disease, prognosis and 
implications of initiating therapy
• Teach safe daily-care skills
Home Care

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 
1Which of the following are clinical
manifestations of ALS? 
Select all that apply.
A. Progressive, unilateral weakness of extremities
Progressive, unilateral muscle weakness and altered respiratory function are indicators of ALS 
due to degenerative changes to upper & lower motor neurons. Pain perception and control of the 
bladder and bowels remain intact. Guillain-Barré Syndrome involves ascending paralysis.
B. Incontinence of bladder and bowels
C. Altered speech, weak cough, and dysphagia
D. Ascending muscle paralysis, beginning with lower 
extremities towards the head
E. Decreased perception to touch or pain

PHYSICAL ASSESSMENT
57-year-old male presents with worsening dysphagia and 
increased fatigue. AXO4, PERRLA. Speech is slowed with 
slurring. He endorses dyspnea on exertion and weak cough. 
Spouse reported drooling. Weakness noted to all 
extremities. Grip strength is 2/5 to right hand and 3/5 to left 
hand. Fasciculations observed to both upper extremities. 
Unsteady gait. Patient ambulates with a cane.
MEDICATION LIST
Amlodipine 5 mg PO daily, Omeprazole 40 mg PO daily, 
Riluzole 50 mg PO BID, Tizanidine 2 mg PO Q8H PRN, 
Baclofen 10 mg PO BID
Potential Condition
NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 2
Rationale: The potential condition is ALS. The nurse 
should  offer the client alternative forms of 
communication and perform passive ROM to prevent 
muscle contractures. Upright positioning promotes 
effective breathing and helps prevent aspiration. Thin 
liquids and dry crackers are contraindicated due to his 
dysphagia.
The nurse must monitor the client's respiratory status. In 
addition, she must monitor liver function tests because 
riluzole is hepatotoxic.
